readings.title: The Land of Little Rain — the author’s preface
readings.challenge: Work out why the author refuses to use map names, and what she offers instead.
readings.focus: Naming a place as a way of knowing it, loving it and protecting it.
readings.context: Mary Austin (1868–1934) wrote The Land of Little Rain (1903), essays on the desert country between California’s Sierra Nevada and Death Valley, where she lived in the Owens Valley around 1900. Kearsarge is a mountain above the town of Independence, where Austin lived; the brown house is her own. Yosemite is a valley in the Sierra Nevada; the Mojave is a desert to the south; “perpetuity” is lasting forever; “wanton” here means someone who gives herself carelessly; to “annex” is to take over territory.
readings.contentNote: Austin generalizes about “the Indian fashion of name-giving” and says Native names are “always beautifully fit”; she means praise, but she describes many different peoples as if they were one.

excerpt.locator: Preface, the whole preface; opens “I confess to a great liking for the Indian fashion of name-giving: every man known by…”; closes “…land, of its trails and what is astir in them, as one lover of it can give to another.”.

questions.prompt: What does Austin mean by “the Indian fashion of name-giving”? Why does she like it?
facilitatorNotes: A person is named by whatever phrase best expresses him to the one who names him, so the same man may have different names to friend and enemy. She likes it because it fits the many sides of a person, and she will name places the same way, by what they mean to her.
evidence: every man known by that phrase which best expresses him to whoso names him.
No other fashion, I think, sets so well with the various natures that inhabit in us,

questions.prompt: Give two reasons she will not use the names on the map. Is she being generous, possessive or both?
facilitatorNotes: The map names often honor discoverers, while she prefers names that describe; and she does not want to send readers to places they will treat “less tenderly” than she does. She jokes that naming lets her “annex” the country to her own estate. Readers can see both love and ownership in that, which is also what renaming land has often meant.
evidence: And I am in no mind to direct you to delectable places toward which you will hold yourself less tenderly than I.
annex to my own estate a very great territory to which none has a surer title.

questions.prompt: “The earth is no wanton to give up all her best to every comer.” According to the preface, how does one come to know this land?
facilitatorNotes: Slowly, by living through its seasons: “One must summer and winter with the land and wait its occasions.” Her examples are plants that take years to ripen or seven years to sprout, which “do not scrape acquaintance” with a visitor on a short vacation.
evidence: One must summer and winter with the land and wait its occasions.
these do not scrape acquaintance.

questions.prompt: The preface ends with directions to a brown house at the end of a village street. Why end with an invitation, after refusing to give directions?
facilitatorNotes: She will not hand out the land to strangers on a map, but she will share it in person with someone who cares, “as one lover of it can give to another.” The ending sets the warm, personal voice of the essays that follow.
evidence: never leave it until you have knocked at the door of the brown house under the willow-tree
as one lover of it can give to another.

readings.title: The Scavengers — buzzards in the dry years
readings.challenge: Notice how Austin mixes disgust, fairness and humor in describing birds most people dislike.
readings.focus: Seeing an unpleasant part of nature clearly, without looking away.
readings.context: Mary Austin (1868–1934) wrote The Land of Little Rain (1903), essays on the desert country between California’s Sierra Nevada and Death Valley, where she lived in the Owens Valley around 1900. Buzzards here are turkey vultures, large birds that eat carrion, the flesh of dead animals; Austin also writes of larger “vultures,” which she tells apart by the white patches under their wings. El Tejon was a great cattle ranch at the south end of the San Joaquin Valley; a mesa is a flat-topped highland; “rack-boned” means so thin the bones show; a quarry is the hunted animal; San Juan Hill was a battle in Cuba in the Spanish–American War of 1898; primaries are a bird’s long wing feathers; offal is waste from slaughtered animals.
readings.contentNote: Austin describes cattle starving to death, a man lost in the desert without water, and the dead after a battle, without dwelling on gore.

excerpt.locator: The Scavengers, from the opening to the vulture’s “bandit airs”; opens “Fifty-seven buzzards, one on each of fifty-seven fence posts at the rancho El Tejon, on a…”; closes “…he is a sombre bird, with none of the buzzard’s frank satisfaction in his offensiveness.”.

questions.prompt: Reread the first paragraph. Which details make the scene feel hot, heavy and grim, and which add a touch of comedy?
facilitatorNotes: The air “breathes like cotton wool,” the birds droop and smell “to heaven,” and they speak in “a rare, horrid croak.” The exact count, fifty-seven birds on fifty-seven posts sitting “solemnly” for three hours, is almost funny. The mix sets the tone of the essay.
evidence: Fifty-seven buzzards, one on each of fifty-seven fence posts
There is no end to them, and they smell to heaven.

questions.prompt: Why does Austin call the death of the cattle “a very squalid tragedy”? What does she suggest about animals and death?
facilitatorNotes: It is slow, ugly starvation, without any grandeur. She thinks the animals understand death almost as well as people, who “have only the more imagination,” and that their quiet after the first fear is a kind of acceptance.
evidence: It is a very squalid tragedy
I suppose the dumb creatures know nearly as much of death as do their betters, who have only the more imagination.

questions.prompt: Austin calls the buzzards both part of “the economy of nature” and “loathsome watchers.” How do the stories of Timmie O’Shea and of Ewan help her hold both views?
facilitatorNotes: Scavengers are useful, but waiting for a creature to die is horrible to imagine, and she makes us imagine it for a man. The stories show that the same birds can be a guide to the lost and a sickening sight after a battle.
evidence: It is doubtless the economy of nature to have the scavengers by to clean up the carrion,
Suppose now it were a man in this long-drawn, hungrily spied upon distress!

questions.prompt: Find places where Austin is fair to the buzzards. Does her humor make her portrait fairer or less fair?
facilitatorNotes: She grants them a “stately flight,” loyalty to their kind and parental pride, and she separates fact from hearsay about vultures. Her jokes judge them by human manners (“crass and simple pride”), which some readers find unfair and others find honest about her own feelings.
evidence: All their offensiveness notwithstanding, they have a stately flight.
full of a crass and simple pride,

readings.title: The Scavengers — the economy of nature
readings.challenge: Follow the essay as it widens from single birds to a whole network of creatures, and then to people.
readings.focus: How Austin turns an essay on scavengers into a judgment of human beings.
readings.context: Recap: Austin has described the buzzards and vultures that gather in dry years to feed on starving cattle, calling their work both necessary and loathsome. The raven, called “carrion crow” locally, is a large black bird; the Shoshone are a Native people of the desert; “arrant” means utter; antelope here are pronghorn; chaparral is dense scrub; “defiles” are narrow passes; shambles were slaughterhouses; Clark’s crow is now called Clark’s nutcracker; to “vituperate” is to scold; a gormand (gourmand) loves food.
readings.contentNote: The essay describes thousands of sheep and cattle dying along a desert road in a drought, and the scavengers feeding on them.

excerpt.locator: The Scavengers, from the raven to the end of the essay; opens “The least objectionable of the inland scavengers is the raven, frequenter of the desert…”; closes “…that eats tin cans, and no wild thing leaves a like disfigurement on the forest floor.”.

questions.prompt: Why does Austin like the raven better than the buzzard? How does the scene at Red Rock end with a joke?
facilitatorNotes: He is handsome, clean in his habits, clever and even playful; a tame one in a camp “could all but talk.” At the carcass shared by buzzards, ravens and a coyote, “only the coyote seemed ashamed of the company,” as if the animals had a sense of social rank.
evidence: He is handsomer and has such an air.
and only the coyote seemed ashamed of the company.

questions.prompt: “Probably we never fully credit the interdependence of wild creatures.” What examples does Austin give, and what question does she leave unanswered?
facilitatorNotes: When coyotes hunt an antelope, an eagle, buzzards and hawks gather “like small boys to a street fight,” and the rabbits feel safe; the hawk follows the badger, the coyote the crow. She asks how much young animals learn by themselves and how much they are taught by their elders.
evidence: hawks came trooping like small boys to a street fight.
how much they are taught of their elders.

questions.prompt: What happened on the road from Mojave to Red Butte? Who is responsible for that feast?
facilitatorNotes: In a drought, people drove thousands of animals across a waterless desert to mountain pasture, and many died on the way. The scavengers “gorged and gorged” on a disaster caused by human decisions, though Austin does not openly blame anyone.
evidence: In the defiles of Red Rock, the sheep piled up a stinking lane;
the scavengers gorged and gorged.

questions.prompt: Read the last paragraph. What is Austin’s final point, and how has the whole essay prepared for it?
facilitatorNotes: Nature’s scavengers clean up everything wild, but nothing eats tin cans: only people leave lasting litter. After pages on how no carcass is wasted, the human mess stands out. Some readers call this an early environmental argument; others notice it is only a closing paragraph.
evidence: Man is a great blunderer going about in the woods,
There is no scavenger that eats tin cans,

readings.title: The Pocket Hunter — a man who takes the color of the land
readings.challenge: Collect the details that make the Pocket Hunter seem part of the landscape.
readings.focus: A character sketch of a prospector who lives by luck and instinct.
readings.context: Mary Austin (1868–1934) wrote The Land of Little Rain (1903), essays on the desert country between California’s Sierra Nevada and Death Valley, where she lived in the Owens Valley around 1900. A pocket hunter searches the hills for small, rich deposits of gold ore; the essay explains the word. Gilias are small desert flowers; a campoodie is a Paiute settlement; “tailorwise” means cross-legged; burros are small donkeys, and hobbles tie their legs loosely so they cannot stray far; a “dry camp” has no water nearby; mesquite is a thorny desert shrub with edible beans; “colors” are specks of gold in a washing pan; a grub staker is given food and supplies in exchange for a share of any find.
readings.contentNote: A man is killed in a flood, and the Pocket Hunter buries him.

excerpt.locator: The Pocket Hunter, from the opening to the flood in Grape-vine Cañon; opens “I remember very well when I first met him. Walking in the evening glow to spy the…”; closes “…but he never laid his own escape at any door but the unintelligible favor of the Powers.”.

questions.prompt: How does Austin describe the Pocket Hunter’s looks and manner? Why compare him to “small hunted things”?
facilitatorNotes: He has a face and speech “of no character at all,” clothes of no fashion, and a wordless hum. Like a small animal, he takes on “the protective color of his surroundings” and blends into the land.
evidence: as if he had that faculty of small hunted things of taking on the protective color of his surroundings.

questions.prompt: “The sensible thing … The logical thing is to set out looking for another one.” What is the joke, and what does it show about the Pocket Hunter?
facilitatorNotes: Sense says quit while you are ahead; the hunter’s “logic” says that if one pocket exists, there must be more. He has followed that logic for twenty years. Austin suggests pocket hunting is less a plan than a calling, something a man is “born with.”
evidence: The logical thing is to set out looking for another one.
I suppose no man becomes a pocket hunter by first intention.

questions.prompt: “The land tolerated him as it might a gopher or a badger. Of all its inhabitants it has the least concern for man.” What view of nature does this give? How does it differ from nature as kind or motherly?
facilitatorNotes: The desert is neither friendly nor cruel, simply indifferent; the hunter survives because he asks nothing and fits in like an animal. Some readers find that freeing; others find it bleak.
evidence: the land tolerated him as it might a gopher or a badger.
Of all its inhabitants it has the least concern for man.

questions.prompt: How did the Pocket Hunter escape the flood? Compare his explanation with Austin’s.
facilitatorNotes: He got up and moved out of the water’s path while still asleep, waking only as the flood went by. He credits “the unintelligible favor of the Powers”; Austin points to “the weather instinct,” which “does not sleep.” Readers can weigh luck, instinct and providence; the neighbor’s death makes the question sharper.
evidence: But the weather instinct does not sleep.
he never laid his own escape at any door but the unintelligible favor of the Powers.

readings.title: The Pocket Hunter — the wild sheep and the green bag
readings.challenge: Notice what Austin values in the Pocket Hunter and what she cannot forgive him.
readings.focus: A wanderer’s dream of respectability, and the pull of the life he knows.
readings.context: Recap: Austin has described the Pocket Hunter, a quiet, bowed prospector who has spent twenty years searching the desert ranges for small pockets of gold, and who once escaped a flood in his sleep. Hot Creek is an area of hot springs and steam vents; piñon pines bear edible nuts; bighorn wild sheep winter in the high mountains; “float” is loose ore broken from a vein; Tonopah, in Nevada, and the Rand district, in California, later became famous mining districts; a “green bag” was the bag English lawyers carried; the Grand Tour was a traditional journey through Europe; “bourgeois” means middle-class; a swale is a low, damp hollow.

excerpt.locator: The Pocket Hunter, from the country beyond Hot Creek to the end of the essay; opens “The journeyings of the Pocket Hunter led him often into that mysterious country beyond…”; closes “…not surprised to find it was the Pocket Hunter. No man can be stronger than his destiny.”.

questions.prompt: Austin finds the hunter’s “accounts” more interesting than his “explanations.” What is the difference, and what does it show about her as an observer?
facilitatorNotes: His accounts are what he saw: the creeks, the piñon crop, the bear fishing in Pine Creek. His explanations mix miners’ talk and superstition. She trusts observation over theory, and she sees something he does not: how much he depends on the animals and trees for a sense of home.
evidence: I always found the accounts he brought me more interesting than his explanations,
I suppose he never knew how much he depended for the necessary sense of home and companionship on the beasts and trees,

questions.prompt: Reread the night among the wild sheep. Which words make the morning feel holy? Why does Austin follow it with the hunter’s prejudices?
facilitatorNotes: “The very soul of him shook to see the wild sheep of God,” the “white pavilions of the snow,” leaps “nearest to flight.” Then she notes that he still believes in toad venom and hates coyotes. Even a man given such a vision may learn nothing true about animals from it, and Austin cannot forgive him the coyote.
evidence: Then the very soul of him shook to see the wild sheep of God stand up about him,
had all the miner’s prejudices against my friend the coyote.

questions.prompt: What was the Pocket Hunter’s ambition in London? How does Austin’s description of the English middle class show what she thinks of it?
facilitatorNotes: He wanted to strike it rich and live among the comfortable middle class. Austin describes that life as having gentility above “to aspire to” and “smaller fry to bully and patronize,” which is a sharp judgment, though she adds that he “did not put it so crudely.”
evidence: to strike it rich and set himself up among the eminently bourgeois of London.
sufficient smaller fry to bully and patronize,

questions.prompt: “No man can be stronger than his destiny.” What happened, and is the ending a failure for the Pocket Hunter or a return to his true life?
facilitatorNotes: He got his ten thousand dollars and went to London, but a year or two later Austin follows a trail of smoke and finds him again by his coffee-pot and frying-pan. Some readers see a dream defeated; others see a man who belongs to the hills going home. The repeated campfire, like the first meeting, suggests the second.
evidence: came upon a man by the fire with a coffee-pot and frying-pan.
No man can be stronger than his destiny.

readings.title: My Neighbor’s Field — owners, plants and a legend
readings.challenge: Compare the field’s legal history with the history written in its plants.
readings.focus: Who really owns a piece of land, and what lasts on it.
readings.context: Mary Austin (1868–1934) wrote The Land of Little Rain (1903), essays on the desert country between California’s Sierra Nevada and Death Valley, where she lived in the Owens Valley around 1900. The Paiutes are the Native people of the Owens Valley. In the early 1860s, as cattlemen and miners moved in, they fought settlers and United States soldiers and were defeated, and many were forced from the valley for a time; Paiute communities still live there today. Kearsarge is the mountain above Austin’s village. A wicket is a small gate; “mesne lords” were, in old English law, lords who held land under a greater lord; to homestead was to claim public land by living on and farming it; middens are old rubbish heaps; sweat-houses were used for ritual sweat baths; obsidian is a black volcanic glass; a rod is about five meters. In the Bible (1 Kings 21) King Ahab covets his neighbor Naboth’s vineyard, and Naboth is killed so the king can take it.
readings.contentNote: Austin calls the shepherds “wild, hairy men of little speech” and retells a Paiute legend in which the pines were “bad Indians”; these are her period descriptions and her version of the story.

excerpt.locator: My Neighbor’s Field, from the opening to the pine cones at Austin’s door; opens “It is one of those places God must have meant for a field from all time, lying very level…”; closes “…and I look, if I live long enough, to see them come up greenly in my neighbor’s field.”.

questions.prompt: Trace how the field passed from Roeder to Ruffin. What is Austin’s attitude toward this story, and how can you tell?
facilitatorNotes: Connor took the field when the loan fell due during the Big Snow; Roeder arrived eighteen days late with the money; the lawsuit ended with the field in the hands of Connor’s own lawyer. Her wry phrases (“took the law by the forelock,” “the tongue to wile a bird out of the bush”) show amused contempt for the greed.
evidence: At the set time Connor took the law by the forelock
Eighteen days later Roeder arrived on snowshoes, both feet frozen, and the money in his pack.

questions.prompt: Why does Austin call her neighbor Naboth? Whom does that make her?
facilitatorNotes: In the Bible story Naboth owns the vineyard that a king envies. Calling her neighbor Naboth casts Austin as the envious king, a self-mocking admission that she covets the field, and a reminder of how many people have wanted it.
evidence: whom from envying his possession I call Naboth.

questions.prompt: “All this human occupancy of greed and mischief left no mark on the field, but the Indians did, and the unthinking sheep.” What marks did they leave?
facilitatorNotes: Arrow points and the remains of camps, and plants out of place: the hoopee and hackberries whose berries the Paiutes ate, and screw-bean mesquite carried as seed on the sheep’s coats. The plants keep a record of who lived there and how.
evidence: Round its corners children pick up chipped arrow points of obsidian,
The seed must have shaken there from some sheep’s coat,

questions.prompt: How does the ending, with the pines returning, answer the story of owners at the start? Is it fair to give the pines a “secret purpose”?
facilitatorNotes: The pines held the field before anyone, and Austin imagines them marching back while legal owners come and go. “Secret purpose” is her fancy, since trees spread by seed and flood, but it makes the point that ownership is brief. Notice the irony of the title phrase in her last words.
evidence: it would seem their secret purpose to regain their old footing.
to see them come up greenly in my neighbor’s field.

readings.title: The Mesa Trail — hunters and burrowers
readings.challenge: Separate what Austin observes from the human character she gives each animal.
readings.focus: A web of hunters, watchers and burrowers on the open mesa.
readings.context: Mary Austin (1868–1934) wrote The Land of Little Rain (1903), essays on the desert country between California’s Sierra Nevada and Death Valley, where she lived in the Owens Valley around 1900. The Paiutes are the Native people of the Owens Valley. In the early 1860s, as cattlemen and miners moved in, they fought settlers and United States soldiers and were defeated, and many were forced from the valley for a time; Paiute communities still live there today. A mesa is a flat-topped highland; the “split-feet” are animals with divided paws; a pot-hunter hunts for food rather than sport; a curmudgeon is a bad-tempered person; a besom is a broom; a campoodie is a Paiute village of brush huts (wattles); chia is a plant whose seeds the Paiutes gathered; “two bits” is a quarter of a dollar; a curio dealer sells souvenirs. The flat “toad-like creature” is a horned lizard.
readings.contentNote: Austin says foxes and coyotes kill “for the pure love of slaughter”; that is her judgment, not established animal science. Her picture of a Paiute camp uses period generalizations.

excerpt.locator: The Mesa Trail, from the red fox and the coyote to the horned lizard; opens “Both the red fox and the coyote are free of the night hours, and both killers for the…”; closes “…of the color of the soil; and the curio dealer will give you two bits for it, to stuff.”.

questions.prompt: How does Austin characterize the coyote and the badger? What do the human labels add, and what might they hide?
facilitatorNotes: The coyote is a garrulous, bold, curious “lord of the mesa”; the badger is a friendless “curmudgeon,” “a pot-hunter and no sportsman.” The labels make the animals vivid and memorable, but they judge animals by human manners.
evidence: The coyote is your real lord of the mesa,
The badger is a pot-hunter and no sportsman.

questions.prompt: Explain how a badger’s hunt feeds the hawks. Why are the hawks “wiser in their generation, though they do not look it”?
facilitatorNotes: When the badger digs into a burrow, the small animals escape by back doors, where the hawks wait. The crows only walk about expecting something; the hawks understand the burrow’s exits.
evidence: When the badger goes down, as many of the furry people as are not caught napping come up by the back doors,
and are wiser in their generation, though they do not look it.

questions.prompt: “It takes man to leave unsightly scars on the face of the earth.” Then Austin calls abandoned Paiute camps “spots of desolation.” Does her example fit her claim?
facilitatorNotes: She seems to count the camps among human scars, though she then explains that the Paiutes choose high ground and let sun and air clean a site before moving on. Readers can argue whether she is criticizing the Paiutes, people in general, or neither.
evidence: It takes man to leave unsightly scars on the face of the earth.
the abandoned campoodies of the Paiutes are spots of desolation

questions.prompt: Why does Austin call the horned lizard’s disappearing act “pure witchcraft”? What does the last detail about the curio dealer add?
facilitatorNotes: The lizard is the color of sand, so a patch of the trail seems to come alive and vanish. Once caught, the magic is gone and it becomes a cheap souvenir “to stuff.” The ending sets wonder against people who see wildlife only as goods.
evidence: This is pure witchcraft.
and the curio dealer will give you two bits for it, to stuff.

readings.title: The Basket Maker — Seyavi’s art
readings.challenge: Follow how Austin builds a portrait of a woman from the land, the year and the baskets she made.
readings.focus: Survival after defeat, and an art that holds a life.
readings.context: Mary Austin (1868–1934) wrote The Land of Little Rain (1903), essays on the desert country between California’s Sierra Nevada and Death Valley, where she lived in the Owens Valley around 1900. The Paiutes are the Native people of the Owens Valley. In the early 1860s, as cattlemen and miners moved in, they fought settlers and United States soldiers and were defeated, and many were forced from the valley for a time; Paiute communities still live there today. Seyavi is a Paiute woman Austin knew. A campoodie is a Paiute village; tule is a marsh reed; a slough is a marshy channel; the tulares are reed marshes; pronghorn are antelope and bighorn are wild sheep; one-leafed pines bear edible nuts; chaparral is dense scrub; “crimping” is waving one’s hair; taboose is an edible root the Paiutes dug.
readings.contentNote: Austin describes the Paiutes’ defeat in war, hints that Paiute women were attacked by the conquerors, and compares Seyavi to a stray dog fending for her pups. She writes of the “dying struggle” of Seyavi’s people and generalizes about “every Indian woman”; these are her period views.

excerpt.locator: The Basket Maker, from the opening to Seyavi’s golden cooking bowls; opens ““A man,” says Seyavi of the campoodie, “must have a woman, but a woman who has a child…”; closes “…with the pattern of plumed quail, you would understand all this without saying anything.”.

questions.prompt: “A man must have a woman, but a woman who has a child will do very well.” What does Seyavi mean, and how did she come to believe it?
facilitatorNotes: A woman with a child to live for has purpose enough. She learned it in the war and famine years, hiding with her son and feeding him on roots and clams, and she found how much more easily “one can do without a man than might at first be supposed.”
evidence: That was the time Seyavi learned the sufficiency of mother wit,
how much more easily one can do without a man than might at first be supposed.

questions.prompt: “To understand the fashion of any life, one must know the land it is lived in and the procession of the year.” How does Austin follow her own rule in this section?
facilitatorNotes: Before describing Seyavi’s art she describes the narrow valley, the river and the lake, and what food each season gave. Seyavi’s endurance makes sense only against that scarcity and the war that made game and hunters warier.
evidence: To understand the fashion of any life, one must know the land it is lived in and the procession of the year.
That was really all they could depend upon,

questions.prompt: Austin compares Seyavi to a stray dog foraging for her litter. Is the comparison respectful?
facilitatorNotes: She clearly admires the dog’s courage and sufficiency, and she admits she is imagining (“since she will not talk of it”). But comparing a Native woman to an animal, in a book that often treats Native people as part of the landscape, can feel demeaning. Both readings can be argued from the passage.
evidence: slinking savage and afraid, remembering and mistrusting humankind, wistful, lean, and sufficient for her young.
since she will not talk of it.

questions.prompt: What gives Seyavi’s baskets “a touch beyond cleverness”? How does the quail pattern connect her art to her life?
facilitatorNotes: She wove the same quail design in her wedding year and again after the war, so the pattern carries her happiness and her recovery. She cut willows only at golden times, so “the soul of the weather went into the wood.” Austin also contrasts making “for love” with selling “for money.”
evidence: In this pattern she had made cooking pots in the golden spring of her wedding year,
Seyavi made baskets for love and sold them for money,

readings.title: The Basket Maker — the end of the basket maker
readings.challenge: Notice the moments when Seyavi answers back, and decide what Austin learns from her.
readings.focus: Home, loss and dignity in old age.
readings.context: Recap: Seyavi, a Paiute woman who survived war and famine and raised her son alone, became a skilled basket maker; Austin admires her bowls patterned with plumed quail. Clematis is a climbing plant with white flowers; Paiutes burned baskets for their dead, much as others lay flowers on graves; Sitka is in Alaska and Samarkand in Central Asia; a reservation is land set aside by the government for a Native people; in the Bible (Judges 4–5) Deborah is a prophet and judge who leads Israel; ichor was the fluid in the veins of the Greek gods; a wickiup is a brush hut; weanlings are young children just weaned; kitchen middens are rubbish heaps; a closet here is a private room for prayer.
readings.contentNote: The passage describes Seyavi’s old age and blindness and calls the Paiutes on the reservation “hangers-on” in a “deplorable condition.” Austin generalizes about “Indian women” and Paiute beliefs; discuss these as her views, not facts.

excerpt.locator: The Basket Maker, from Seyavi’s dancing days to the end of the essay; opens “Before Seyavi made baskets for the satisfaction of desire,--for that is a house-bred…”; closes “…that having borne herself courageously to this end she will not be reborn a coyote.”.

questions.prompt: “What good will your dead get, Seyavi, of the baskets you burn?” What does Seyavi’s answer do to Austin’s question?
facilitatorNotes: Austin asks partly because she wants the baskets for her collection. Seyavi turns the question back: Austin’s flowers on graves are no more useful. Austin records herself being answered, and the reader sees that both customs are acts of love, not practical ones.
evidence: said I, coveting them for my own collection.
As much good as yours of the flowers you strew.

questions.prompt: According to Austin, what is a Paiute’s home, and why can homesickness be “unto death”? What does this suggest about being moved to a reservation?
facilitatorNotes: Home is the land itself: the hills, winds and stream, which cannot be bought again elsewhere. Moving away from them is a loss with no relief. Austin also shows that people on the reservation still laugh and tell tales, so her “hangers-on” is not the whole picture.
evidence: Not the wattled hut is his home, but the land, the winds, the hill front, the stream.
Yet you hear them laughing

questions.prompt: Why might Austin compare Seyavi in her best days to Deborah? How does that change our sense of her?
facilitatorNotes: Deborah was a wise leader of her people. The comparison gives Seyavi authority and dignity, “quick in counsel, slow of speech, esteemed of her people,” rather than presenting her only as a survivor or a craftswoman.
evidence: In her best days Seyavi was most like Deborah,
esteemed of her people.

questions.prompt: Read the last paragraph. How does Austin compare Seyavi’s hope with her readers’? Does the ending honor Seyavi or keep her at a distance?
facilitatorNotes: Austin says Seyavi knows “quite as much” about life’s meaning as readers with “a larger hope” of heaven, though her only certainty is that her courage will save her from being reborn a coyote. Some readers find this a tribute to her courage; others notice that Austin still speaks for Seyavi, who is never asked.
evidence: she knows in fact quite as much of these matters as you who have a larger hope,
she will not be reborn a coyote.

readings.title: Water Borders — from the snow to the ditch
readings.challenge: Read the long sentence about the stream aloud, and listen to how it moves.
readings.focus: Life at the edge of the high snow, where only the humble thrive.
readings.context: Mary Austin (1868–1934) wrote The Land of Little Rain (1903), essays on the desert country between California’s Sierra Nevada and Death Valley, where she lived in the Owens Valley around 1900. This passage describes the high Sierra near timber-line, the height above which trees cannot grow. Gilias, polymonium (polemonium), primroses, mimulus and columbine are mountain flowers; carmine is crimson; a pot-hole is a round hollow worn in rock by water; catkins are soft spikes of tiny flowers; manzanita is a shrub with small red fruit; a sward is turf; the white-bark pine and the tamarack (lodgepole) pine are mountain conifers. In Charles Dickens’s novel Oliver Twist, the hungry orphan Oliver asks for more food.
readings.contentNote: Austin finds the horns of a young wild sheep caught in a tree and imagines its slow death.

excerpt.locator: Water Borders, from the flowers above the lakes to the sheep’s horns at Windy Lake; opens “Since no lake can be at the highest point, it is possible to find plant life higher than…”; closes “…to the long agony, but we could not be sure. I never liked the spit of Windy Lake again.”.

questions.prompt: Reread the sentence that begins “It slips stilly by.” List its verbs. How does the sentence imitate the stream?
facilitatorNotes: Slips, drops, gathers itself, plunges, roars, foams and bridles, glides, tumbles, curdles: the pace changes from quiet to wild to calm and back, and the sentence keeps going, clause after clause, until the stream reaches “steadier going.”
evidence: It slips stilly by the glacier scoured rim of an ice bordered pool,
and so arrives at the open country and steadier going.

questions.prompt: What is the dwarf willow’s “business,” and why does Austin admire how it does it?
facilitatorNotes: To flower and set seed in a very short season. It hugs the ground, roots wherever it can, and spends almost nothing on leaves and stems, so it “rarely” fails. It shows the economy that survival demands at that height.
evidence: No other plant of high altitudes knows its business so well.
It hugs the ground,

questions.prompt: “It does not do to be anything but humble in the alpine regions, but not fearful.” How does Austin apply this to herself, and what is her joke about Oliver Twist?
facilitatorNotes: She has spent hours in cold meadows where one might expect to “get one’s death” and come to no harm, except hunger: Oliver Twist’s complaint. The joke keeps the advice light and practical.
evidence: It does not do to be anything but humble in the alpine regions, but not fearful.
except it might be Oliver Twist’s complaint.

questions.prompt: What did Austin find on the spit of Windy Lake, and why did she never like the place again? How does the passage move from humor to this?
facilitatorNotes: A young sheep had caught its horns in a pine, and the tree had grown over them. She hoped a predator ended its agony quickly but “could not be sure.” The quiet ending shows that her delight in mountain life includes feeling for its suffering; the stillness of timber-line now has a shadow.
evidence: a pair of sheep’s horns not fully grown caught in the crotch of a pine
I never liked the spit of Windy Lake again.

readings.title: The Land of Little Rain — the land that calls men back
readings.challenge: Test a general claim against the one story offered to prove it, and notice whose deaths the story counts.
readings.focus: Why people stay in a land that punishes them.
readings.context: Mary Austin (1868–1934) wrote The Land of Little Rain (1903), essays on the desert country between California’s Sierra Nevada and Death Valley, where she lived in the Owens Valley around 1900. This passage ends the book’s first essay, which describes the desert between the Sierra Nevada and Death Valley. The “lotus charm” recalls the lotus-eaters of Homer’s Odyssey, who ate a fruit that made them forget home. Ores and earths are minerals; borax is a mineral that was mined in Death Valley and hauled out by teams of twenty mules; Mojave was a railroad town; a swamper was a teamster’s helper; Indian Wells was a stop on the desert stage road. “Coolies” was a contemptuous name for Chinese and other Asian labourers.
readings.contentNote: Austin reports without comment that some labourers died each hot season on the borax road, and uses the offensive word “coolies.”

excerpt.locator: The Land of Little Rain, the last three paragraphs of the opening essay; opens “If one is inclined to wonder at first how so many dwellers came to be in the loneliest…”; closes “…moon, looming through the golden dust above his eighteen mules. The land had called him.”.

questions.prompt: According to Austin, why do people come to the loneliest land and stay? Find two reasons.
facilitatorNotes: It “lays such a hold on the affections”; its beauty “tricks the sense of time,” so you always mean to leave and never do; it has the cleanest air anywhere; and its unreachable mineral wealth bewitches people into trying the impossible.
evidence: None other than this long brown land lays such a hold on the affections.
you always mean to go away without quite realizing that you have not done it

questions.prompt: What do the details of Salty Williams’s mule teams show about what the land costs?
facilitatorNotes: Mules maddened by the clank of a water bucket, a line of shallow graves, men struck down at the noon halt. Salty’s “curses of pacification” delivered in “a level, uninterested voice” show a man who has grown used to it.
evidence: dealing out curses of pacification in a level, uninterested voice
There was a line of shallow graves along that road

questions.prompt: The teamsters “used to count on dropping a man or two of every new gang of coolies.” What does Austin’s flat way of reporting this suggest, and how might a reader respond?
facilitatorNotes: The labourers’ deaths were expected, almost planned for, and their lives treated as cheap. Austin records it without comment, while Salty’s swamper, a man with a name to his crew, gets stones against coyotes and a headboard she reads seven years later. Readers can notice the difference in how the dead are remembered and question it.
evidence: they used to count on dropping a man or two of every new gang of coolies
still bright and unweathered

questions.prompt: Salty quits because the road is too hot. How does the last short paragraph answer the question the passage began with?
facilitatorNotes: She meets him again, ruddy and cheerful, driving eighteen mules across Indian Wells: “The land had called him.” The story proves her claim that men curse the land and go back to it.
evidence: Salty quit his job
The land had called him.

readings.title: Water Trails of the Ceriso — what the spring reveals
readings.challenge: Follow Austin as she reconstructs what happened at night from what she finds by day.
readings.focus: Indirect evidence: tracks, trails and the hunters that reveal their prey.
readings.context: Mary Austin (1868–1934) wrote The Land of Little Rain (1903), essays on the desert country between California’s Sierra Nevada and Death Valley, where she lived in the Owens Valley around 1900. Water Trails of the Ceriso follows the paths desert animals wear to a small spring; the Ceriso is a shallow basin near her home. A maverick is an unbranded calf; vaqueros are cowboys; a yearling is a year-old animal; the cougar, puma and mountain lion are the same animal; the small fry are small creatures; spermophiles are ground squirrels; the elf owls here are small owls that live in burrows; a hummock is a small mound; the mesa is a flat-topped upland.
readings.contentNote: A cougar’s kill and owls hunting at night are described.

excerpt.locator: Water Trails of the Ceriso, the paragraphs on the cattle, the cougar’s kill and the small creatures at the spring; opens “Cattle, when there are any in the Ceriso, drink morning and evening, spending the night…”; closes “…to frighten them into some near-by burrow, it is possible to trail them far up the slope.”.

questions.prompt: What older habit do the half-wild cattle keep, and how does Austin know it is an old one?
facilitatorNotes: They turn round and round before lying down, “as dogs do,” though they have long stopped making beds. A habit that no longer serves a purpose points back to “an earlier lineage,” wild ancestors.
evidence: In these half wild spotted steers the habits of an earlier lineage persist.
before lying down they turn themselves round and round as dogs do

questions.prompt: How does Austin work out the cougar’s night from what she finds in the morning? List her evidence and her conclusions.
facilitatorNotes: Evidence: a half-eaten yearling at the foot of the rock and pad-prints by the spring. Conclusions: the kill was early; the cat came to drink twice; because a meat-eater drinks little until it has eaten, it must have fed, drunk, rested in the rocks, then eaten and drunk again; the coyotes took the rest. Notice her care: “it appeared,” “must have,” “There was no knowing.”
evidence: the foot-pads of a cougar, puma, mountain lion, or whatever the beast is rightly called
since the meat-eater drinks little until he has eaten

questions.prompt: Austin admits nobody knows when the small creatures visit the spring. What evidence does she use instead of watching them?
facilitatorNotes: The trails themselves, traced miles out through the grass; a few moonlit sightings; and above all the elf owls, which do not care for water, so their gathering near the spring shows that their prey gathers there. She reasons from the hunters to the hunted.
evidence: for evidence of their frequent coming there are the trails
Their presence near the spring in great numbers would indicate the presence of the things they feed upon.

questions.prompt: “All night the rustle and soft hooting keeps on … with seldom small shrieks of mortal agony.” How does this sentence change the picture of the spring?
facilitatorNotes: The place of water and life is also a hunting ground; soft sounds cover killing, and “seldom” means rarely, so the deaths come now and then. The calm tone treats death as part of the order. Readers may find it beautiful or chilling; compare her phrase for the owls, “fluffs of greediness.”
evidence: with seldom small shrieks of mortal agony
Those burrow-haunting, speckled fluffs of greediness

readings.title: Shoshone Land — Winnenap´’s country
readings.challenge: Notice whose memory shapes the description, and when Austin turns from land and plants to people.
readings.focus: A homeland seen through an exile’s longing; how a land shapes the life lived in it.
readings.context: Mary Austin (1868–1934) wrote The Land of Little Rain (1903), essays on the desert country between California’s Sierra Nevada and Death Valley, where she lived in the Owens Valley around 1900. The Paiutes are the Native people of the Owens Valley. In the early 1860s, as cattlemen and miners moved in, they fought settlers and United States soldiers and were defeated, and many were forced from the valley for a time; Paiute communities still live there today. The Shoshones are a neighbouring desert people to the south and east. Winnenap´ (Austin’s spelling) was a Paiute medicine-man, a healer and spiritual leader, who had been born a Shoshone. A campoodie is a Paiute village; the Bitter Lake is Owens Lake; a hostage here is someone handed over to guarantee a peace; interminable means endless; ceanothus and manzanita are shrubs; the bighorn is the mountain sheep and the wapiti the elk; mesquite and creosote are desert shrubs; piñon is a nut pine; a wickiup is a brush hut and wattled means woven of branches; “those that journeyed eastward from Eden” are Adam and Eve and their descendants; viscid means sticky; winnowed sand has been sorted by the wind.
readings.contentNote: Austin, a white writer of 1903, generalizes about “an Indian” and compares a people to plants and birds; readers should question these judgments. Her picture of Winnenap´ comes from his stories as she remembered them.

excerpt.locator: Shoshone Land, from the opening through the doves of the desert spring; opens “It is true I have been in Shoshone Land, but before that, long before, I had seen it…”; closes “…brush shelters from which the Shoshones shot arrows at them when the doves came to drink.”.

questions.prompt: Austin says she will always see Shoshone Land through Winnenap´’s eyes. Why? What does the first paragraph tell us about him?
facilitatorNotes: Before she went there she heard him describe its “happy places one by one, like little blessed islands in a sea of talk.” Born a Shoshone, he lives among the Paiutes with a Paiute name, wife and children, yet longs for home and despises his hosts. Her picture of the land is shaped by a homesick man’s memory.
evidence: like little blessed islands in a sea of talk
Once a Shoshone always a Shoshone.

questions.prompt: How does Austin know that Winnenap´ secretly goes home each year?
facilitatorNotes: Officially he has not seen it since he became a hostage, but each spring he goes to the mountains “to gather herbs” and comes back with “new fortitude” and new details in his stories. She infers the visit from changes in his face and talk; she never says he told her. He keeps the old agreement “to save his honor.”
evidence: the new color of his reminiscences that he had been alone and unspied upon in Shoshone Land
to save his honor and the word of his vanished kin

questions.prompt: “The mesquite is God’s best thought in all this desertness.” What makes the mesquite so admirable to Austin?
facilitatorNotes: Thorny, stocky and “iron-rooted,” it keeps growing as blown sand buries it, its twigs green on top of the dunes while the trunk, thick as an oak, lies fifteen or twenty feet down: “one digs for large timber.” It stands for endurance and adaptation.
evidence: The mesquite is God’s best thought in all this desertness.
In Shoshone Land one digs for large timber

questions.prompt: “The Shoshones live like their trees, with great spaces between.” How does Austin connect land, plants and people? Is the comparison a compliment, and is it fair?
facilitatorNotes: Where there is “room enough and time enough,” trees grow into perfect domes; families live apart by springs and gather once a year; solitude breeds a “well-roundedness and sufficiency.” She admires their self-sufficiency. But comparing a people to plants, or to birds returning to nests, can make them seem part of the scenery rather than people with a history; she mentions only in passing that “now there are no wars.” Readers can weigh both.
evidence: The manner of the country makes the usage of life there
The Shoshones live like their trees, with great spaces between

readings.title: Shoshone Land — the medicine-man’s condition
readings.challenge: Follow a shift from adventure and travel advice to a death, and judge how Austin tells it.
readings.focus: An honour with a deadly condition; grief, fear and blame in an epidemic.
readings.context: Recap: Austin has been describing Shoshone Land, a desert country south of the Owens Valley, as she first knew it through the homesick stories of Winnenap´, a Shoshone-born medicine-man living among the Paiutes as the hostage of an old peace. A residuum is what is left over; chuck-wallas are large lizards; Gopherus agassizii is the desert tortoise; withes are flexible twigs; prerogatives are special rights; jurisdiction is the area of someone’s authority; a sweat-house is a lodge heated for healing; remissness is neglect of duty; to cajole is to coax; “pacific” means peace-loving and a humbug is a fraud; to acquiesce is to accept; jacinth, jasper and chalcedony are jewels from the Bible’s description of heaven.
readings.contentNote: In an epidemic half the children of a village die, and Winnenap´ and other medicine-men are killed by their own people, blamed for the deaths; the killing is told briefly. Austin writes of “savageness” and calls a Paiute orator a “humbug”: the judgments of a white observer of 1903.

excerpt.locator: Shoshone Land, from “Now as to these same Shoshones” to the end of the essay; opens “Now as to these same Shoshones there are some who claim that they have no right to the…”; closes “…and yet no hymn-book heaven, but the free air and free spaces of Shoshone Land.”.

questions.prompt: Retell the story of the buzzards’ eggs. Why might Winnenap´ tell it “with a quaking relish”?
facilitatorNotes: As boys he and a friend crossed the forbidden border to rob buzzard nests for fun; a Paiute hunting party cut them off, and they crept home all day in terror, while he carried the eggs in his garment the whole way. The relish is pride in danger survived and amusement at the absurd treasure. Austin uses it to show children who learn “to be still.”
evidence: always in a sweat of fear
carried those buzzard’s eggs in the slack of his single buckskin garment!

questions.prompt: What is the “honor with a condition” of being a medicine-man? How had Winnenap´ protected himself?
facilitatorNotes: If three patients die, he must give up his office and his life; wounds do not count, but diseases are taken for witchcraft. He refused patients the white doctor had treated, blamed evil spirits in advance, or hid, as he did during the measles while half the children died. Austin admires his cunning, but the image of the graves is grim.
evidence: an honor with a condition
All else failing, he can hide.

questions.prompt: Compare what happened at Three Pines and Tunawai with what happened at Maverick. What made the difference?
facilitatorNotes: Elsewhere younger men’s doubts about old customs, white officials, an orator and townspeople’s food delayed the sentences until the sickness passed. At Maverick there was “no school, no oratory, and no alleviation”: a third of the village died and the rest killed the medicine-men. Delay and outside help mattered; grief and fear, not cruelty, drove the killing. Readers may notice how favourably Austin presents the whites’ part.
evidence: so judgment halted between sentence and execution
But here at Maverick there was no school, no oratory, and no alleviation.

questions.prompt: How does Winnenap´ meet his death, and why does Austin end by imagining his heaven? What does the last sentence say about him, and about her?
facilitatorNotes: He waits apart to meet it “as became a Shoshone,” looking out toward his homeland; his killers need drink to do it. Her imagined heaven is “no hymn-book heaven” but Shoshone Land itself, so in the end he goes home. It shows her respect for him and for a sense of the sacred rooted in a place. Some readers find the ending consoling; others feel it softens a brutal death.
evidence: looked out over Shoshone Land, breathing evenly
but the free air and free spaces of Shoshone Land

readings.title: A Bret Harte Town — the road to Jimville
readings.challenge: Hear the humour in Austin’s description, and notice what she refuses to dramatize.
readings.focus: A real mining town measured against the West of fiction.
readings.context: Mary Austin (1868–1934) wrote The Land of Little Rain (1903), essays on the desert country between California’s Sierra Nevada and Death Valley, where she lived in the Owens Valley around 1900. Bret Harte (1836–1902) made his name with stories of California gold-mining camps, such as “The Luck of Roaring Camp” and “The Outcasts of Poker Flat,” then left the West in 1871 and went on writing about it from the East and Europe. Austin’s essay describes a mining town of her own day under the name Jimville. Forty-niners were the gold-rush miners of 1849; Vasquez was a California bandit of the 1870s; express messengers guarded the mail and gold on stage-coaches; scoriæ are lava cinders; a league is about three miles; a maw is a throat; to gloze over is to disguise; auriferous means gold-bearing; a smelter melts ore to extract the metal; a strike is a rich find of ore; Aurora was a Nevada mining town; bane means ruin.
readings.contentNote: The ravine’s name uses “squaw,” an old word for a Native American woman that is now considered offensive, and Austin uses it as the miners did. The story of the name tells of a Native woman abandoned by her white partner, her drinking, and her death after giving birth.

excerpt.locator: Jimville: A Bret Harte Town, from the opening through the naming of Squaw Gulch; opens “When Mr. Harte found himself with a fresh palette and his particular local color fading…”; closes “…for I know what is best for you; you shall blow out this bubble from your own breath.”.

questions.prompt: Austin begins by saying Bret Harte “should have gone to Jimville.” What is her complaint about him?
facilitatorNotes: He took away his early impression of the West and worked it up “untroubled by any newer fact,” writing from memory and invention rather than observation. Jimville, she says, has more tales and better ones. She sets herself up as the observer of the real thing.
evidence: carried his young impression away to be worked out untroubled by any newer fact
He should have gone to Jimville.

questions.prompt: How does Austin make the journey to Jimville sound both romantic and ridiculous?
facilitatorNotes: Old stage-coaches “far gone in the odor of romance,” once held up by bandits, are mended with wire on the road, so that the whole country seems “held together by wire”; seven passengers squeeze into seats for five among sacks of grain; sheep graze in the mouth of an old volcano, “silly pastoral gentleness” over “elemental violence.”
evidence: all that country and Jimville are held together by wire
a kind of silly pastoral gentleness that glozes over an elemental violence

questions.prompt: What do the Silver Dollar saloon and the story of the town’s name tell you about Jimville?
facilitatorNotes: Silver dollars once set in the bar were pried out “when the glory departed”: a boom gone bust. Three hundred people keep four bars, “though you are not to argue anything from that.” The name came by accident from three Jims and a sign chalked on a tent: practical, unplanned, comic.
evidence: but the proprietor pried them out when the glory departed
though you are not to argue anything from that

questions.prompt: Austin says Bret Harte “would have given you a tale” about Squaw Gulch, but she is “a mere recorder.” How does she tell the story, and why stop where she does?
facilitatorNotes: Briefly and plainly, “the bald way”: Jim Calkins found the dying woman, buried her, carried the baby eighteen miles to Poso, then came back and found his mine, which he took as a reward. She will not milk the feeling, and leaves the reader to “blow out this bubble” from their own breath. Readers may notice that the woman has no name of her own, only an insulting label, while the man who left her is plainly blamed.
evidence: The milk of human kindness, like some wine, must not be uncorked too much in speech lest it lose savor.
you shall blow out this bubble from your own breath

readings.title: A Bret Harte Town — the point of view of Jimville
readings.challenge: Work out a community’s unwritten rules from its anecdotes, then weigh Austin’s praise of them.
readings.focus: Honour, loyalty and indifference: what Austin admires in a lawless-looking town.
readings.context: Recap: Mary Austin has taken us by stage-coach to Jimville, a worn mining town in the California desert that she thinks Bret Harte should have written about, and has told how the town and its gulch got their names. Poker Flat and John Oakhurst, the gentleman gambler, come from Harte’s “The Outcasts of Poker Flat,” and “Brown of Calaveras” is another Harte story with a gambler hero. Faro is a card game; a posse is a band gathered to help a sheriff catch someone; a circuit rider is a preacher who travels between towns; a kinetoscope was an early moving-picture machine, and the Passion Play shows the suffering and death of Jesus; derelicts are abandoned ships, here worn-out men; contact and mother lode are where ore is found; a hoodoo is a curse; St. Jerome was a Christian scholar who lived as a hermit in the desert; perquisites are rights that come with a position.
readings.contentNote: Killings, drunkenness and a gambler’s women are mentioned matter-of-factly; one anecdote concerns a man shot for pursuing another man’s wife.

excerpt.locator: Jimville: A Bret Harte Town, from the town’s conventions to the end of the essay; opens “You could never get into any proper relation to Jimville unless you could slough off and…”; closes “…like the point of view of Jimville. The only difference will be in the decorations.”.

questions.prompt: “You are respected in as much ground as you can shoot over.” What are Jimville’s rules of behaviour, according to Austin?
facilitatorNotes: Almost anything is allowed “a good fellow, one no liar, a free spender, and a backer of his friends’ quarrels.” Jimville judges by a point of honour and by what people have actually done, not by appearances or a good story.
evidence: Almost every latitude of behavior is allowed a good fellow
At Jimville they see behavior as history and judge it by facts

questions.prompt: Explain the “crude equity” in the way Jimville treated Wilkins. Does it make sense to you?
facilitatorNotes: He had shot a man fairly in an open quarrel. People shook his hand because they “had not been officially notified,” and he bought a pincushion at the church fair; but when the sheriff, a Jimville man, came after him, Jimville formed a posse and brought him back. Loyalty to persons governs both the kindness and the arrest. Readers may find it fair, comic or contradictory.
evidence: because we had not been officially notified
because the sheriff was a Jimville man and we had to stand by him.

questions.prompt: Why does Austin give the talk about the Mariposa mine as dialogue? What is funny, or disturbing, about it?
facilitatorNotes: She refuses to “write up” these tales and lets the speech show how flatly they are told: a shooting over a wife and a planned revenge come up only to explain a cheap sale. “Huh!” says Jim Jenkins, and the story rolls on. Violence is ordinary here, “told austerely without imagination.”
evidence: I took it off’n Tom Beatty, cheap, after his brother Bill was shot.
and the tale flows smoothly on.

questions.prompt: In the last paragraphs Austin finds something “pure Greek” in Jimville. What quality does she admire? Do you agree that it is admirable?
facilitatorNotes: An indifference to empty talk and envy, “the courage to sheer off what is not worth while,” endurance without self-pity and no fear of death, like beasts, a desert saint or ancient gods; she predicts the rest of us will end up at Jimville’s point of view, with different “decorations.” Readers may admire its simplicity or object that the same indifference accepts killing and drunkenness, which she lists in the same sentence.
evidence: It is pure Greek in that it represents the courage to sheer off what is not worth while.
The only difference will be in the decorations.

readings.title: Other Water Borders — the ditch and its followers
readings.challenge: Watch Austin move from water to people to plants, and notice how she gives each of them a character.
readings.focus: How water, and the right to it, shapes both people and plants in a dry land.
readings.context: Mary Austin (1868–1934) wrote The Land of Little Rain (1903), essays on the desert country between California’s Sierra Nevada and Death Valley, where she lived in the Owens Valley around 1900. In the dry valleys, ranchers led water from the mountain streams along ditches to their fields, and a water-right was the legal right to a share of a stream. A headgate is the gate that lets water from a stream into a ditch, and a weir a low dam; the Eclipse and the Twisted Dyke are local landmarks; a Winchester is a rifle; manslaughter is a killing judged less guilty than murder; frau is German for wife; a flume is a wooden channel for water; usurpation is seizing a place that belongs to others; premeditation is planning ahead; clematis is a climbing vine and horehound a bitter herb; a febrifuge is a medicine for fever; the mission fathers were the Spanish Catholic priests of California’s missions, and neophytes were their new Native converts; ultramontane means beyond the mountains; tule is a marsh reed and taboose an edible root.
readings.contentNote: In a quarrel over water a rancher shoots dead his neighbour Jesus Montaña, and Austin remarks drily that the killer “had the racial advantage.” She also uses the offensive word “coolies” for Chinese labourers.

excerpt.locator: Other Water Borders, from the opening to the reed that makes a passable sugar; opens “It is the proper destiny of every considerable stream in the west to become an irrigating…”; closes “…and strong for shafts or arrows, affords sweet sap and pith which makes a passable sugar.”.

questions.prompt: “It would seem the streams are willing.” How does Austin treat the streams in the first paragraph? What does she say you need in order to understand a waterway?
facilitatorNotes: She gives them wills and moods: they go “as far as they can, or dare,” and once tamed are like “very busy people” with no time to reveal themselves. To know a ditch you must have known it as a brook and lived beside it, hearing its morning and evening “crooning.”
evidence: like very busy people they have no time to reveal themselves
One needs to have known an irrigating ditch when it was a brook

questions.prompt: Austin calls Judson’s killing of Montaña part of “the Homeric age of settlement.” Compare what happened after that killing with what happened when a Clark shot a Judson twelve years later. What is Austin suggesting about justice on the frontier?
facilitatorNotes: Montaña’s death simply “passed into tradition,” while the later killing brought a jury verdict of manslaughter. Read with “the racial advantage,” the contrast suggests the first killer went unpunished because of who his victim was. “Homeric,” a word for heroic legend, is bitterly ironic; readers can discuss whether her dry joking tone makes the point sharper or treats a death too lightly.
evidence: you can see at once that Judson had the racial advantage
but the jury found for manslaughter

questions.prompt: How is the quarrel over Tule Creek finally settled? Why is the scene comic after so much shooting?
facilitatorNotes: Diedrick’s wife sits on the headgate all day with a long-handled shovel, knitting, while the children bring her dinner; Amos is “too much of a gentleman to fight a lady.” A quiet, stubborn woman ends what rifles could not, and next year a water gauge shares the water “in equal inches.”
evidence: There on the headgate sat Diedrick’s frau with a long-handled shovel across her lap
took the summer ebb in equal inches

questions.prompt: Austin compares the confined water to “a middle-aged and serious neighbor who has had that in his life to make him so.” How does this image connect the water to the human story she has just told?
facilitatorNotes: The water that was fought over has a “brooding” quiet, as if it remembers; the quarrels, “more squalid” or “more tragic,” are part of what it has lived through. Austin suggests you cannot know the water without knowing the people’s struggles over it.
evidence: as one might become aware of a middle-aged and serious neighbor who has had that in his life to make him so
It is the repose of the completely accepted instinct.

questions.prompt: Which plants follow the water toward people, and which keep away? How does Austin give them personalities?
facilitatorNotes: Willows push “a bit farther on the slightest provocation”; the birch is shy and “conservative”; the clematis will not grow in any garden plot; the horehound “hankers after hedgerows.” The ditch is an “impartial distributer” of weeds from far away, and the useful plants seem to make “their services an excuse for the intrusion.”
evidence: The willows go as far as the stream goes, and a bit farther on the slightest provocation.
will not be persuaded to grow in any garden plot
as if they made their services an excuse for the intrusion

readings.title: Other Water Borders — iris fields and the tulares
readings.challenge: Follow the water downhill to its last stop, and notice where Austin says she does not know.
readings.focus: Plants and birds of the wet places, and the mystery of the reed marshes.
readings.context: Mary Austin (1868–1934) wrote The Land of Little Rain (1903), essays on the desert country between California’s Sierra Nevada and Death Valley, where she lived in the Owens Valley around 1900. Earlier in this essay Austin describes how mountain streams are led off into irrigating ditches, and the plants that follow the water toward people. Here she goes on downhill. Weirs are low dams; helenum (Austin’s spelling) is a golden, daisy-like flower; sessile leaves have no stalks; trepidation is trembling; articulation is clear speech; columbine, potentilla and asphodel are flowers; a mesa or bench is a flat tableland; a fault is a crack where land has slipped; swales are low wet hollows; ethereal means airy, heavenly; a composite is a daisy-like flower; Cascara sagrada is Spanish for “sacred bark”; alkali is a bitter salt in the soil; mucilaginous means slimy; tulares are great marshes of tule reeds; a quagmire is a bog; a myriad is a countless number; saffron is orange-yellow; the bittern is a marsh bird with a booming call; fens are marshes. Winnenap´ (Austin’s spelling) was a Paiute medicine-man she knew.

excerpt.locator: Other Water Borders, from the golden helenum flowers by the village weirs to the end of the essay; opens “On, down from the lower lakes to the village weirs, the brown and golden disks of…”; closes “…have swallowed up. What they do there, how fare, what find, is the secret of the tulares.”.

questions.prompt: The helenum flowers tremble “always at the point of breaking into flight,” and the water’s babble “always approaches articulation but never quite achieves it.” What do these two comparisons have in common?
facilitatorNotes: Both are things on the edge of becoming something more alive: flowers almost birds, water almost speech. Austin listens to the land as if it were about to tell her something, a hope the essay’s last paragraph returns to.
evidence: that seems always at the point of breaking into flight
just as the babble of the watercourses always approaches articulation but never quite achieves it

questions.prompt: What is Austin’s complaint about plant names, and what does she notice about buttercups and cowslips?
facilitatorNotes: Calling a plant “false” blames it for not being another plant; the asphodel is “a true lily” and deserves better. English-speaking children give the old loved names to whatever new flower looks nearest, so five unrelated plants are called buttercups. Names show people’s habits more than the plants’ natures.
evidence: The asphodel is at least no falsifier
I am convinced that English-speaking children will always have buttercups.

questions.prompt: “A very poet’s flower, I thought.” What does Austin think the iris is good for, and how does Winnenap´ surprise her? What is the joke on herself?
facilitatorNotes: She thinks it useless, a nuisance in pastures and therefore “needing to be the more loved,” only for looking at. Then she sees Winnenap´ pull a strong fibre from its leaf for snares. The poet’s admiration and the Paiute’s practical knowledge see the same plant very differently, and she lets the moment undercut her.
evidence: A very poet’s flower, I thought;
a fine strong fibre for making snares

questions.prompt: Find two ugly or unpleasant places in this section. Does Austin find anything good in them?
facilitatorNotes: The alkali pools are “black and evil-smelling like old blood,” yet there the true heliotrope grows, with healing sap. The tulares are pale or “poisonous-looking,” rotting and full of malaria, yet slowly “reclaim the land” and shelter blackbirds and wild fowl. She keeps finding life and use in what looks like waste.
evidence: black and evil-smelling like old blood
they raise little islands from the bog and reclaim the land

questions.prompt: “That is why we have meant to explore them and have never done so.” Why does Austin end the essay with what she does not know? Is it a satisfying ending?
facilitatorNotes: The marsh keeps its secret: she hears the birds, but gets “no nearer speech” from them. After a whole essay of close knowledge she admits a limit, which some readers find humble and true, and others a teasing, unfinished close. It echoes the water that never quite speaks.
evidence: The tulares are full of mystery and malaria.
is the secret of the tulares
